headline: Stock Rout Sends Mortgage Rates to Weekly Drop as Bonds Rally
tileReason: The daily 30-year average fell to 7.33% Friday from 7.50% a week earlier as investors fled a stock selloff for the safety of bonds.
takeaway:
Rates ended the week lower. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average closed Friday at 7.33%, down 0.17% from 7.50% the Friday before, after peaking at 7.51% Monday. Most of the drop came Friday, a 0.12% fall in one day after four days of small moves. Freddie Mac's weekly survey rose to 7.28% Thursday, but that survey runs behind and was catching up with the jump in rates earlier this month.

A stock selloff did most of the work. The S&P 500 fell six days in a row, including about 2% Thursday, as worries grew that companies are overspending on artificial intelligence. When investors sell stocks they often buy Treasury bonds for safety, and the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, slid from 5.15% to 5.05% by Thursday's close and to roughly 4.92% Friday afternoon, its first dip below 5% in more than a week.

Other forces pulled both ways. Oil fell to its lowest close since late August, factory surveys in New York and Philadelphia weakened, consumers said they expect less inflation over the next year (3.7%, down from 4.3%), and builder confidence sank to its lowest since 2012; all of that helps rates. Pushing the other way: inflation reports keep running hot, shoppers kept spending, and Fed officials spent the week talking about more rate increases.

Lenders finally passed the rally along on Friday. Bonds improved through the week, but much of it came after lenders had set their rates each day, so the daily average barely moved until Friday's catch-up. Mortgage rates also sit unusually far above Treasuries (about 2.19% for the Optimal Blue index on Nov 17, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%), which leaves lenders room to lower rates further if bonds hold their gains.

A December Fed hike is still expected. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, put the odds of a quarter-point increase in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 at about 90% to 94% late in the week, with the rest on a bigger half-point move after Governor Waller raised that idea. Minutes of the October meeting showed almost all officials expect more increases. These are market expectations, not a Fed forecast.

Next week is short but busy. Bond markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and are expected to close early Friday, so the big data lands Wednesday, Nov 25: the Fed's preferred inflation gauge (PCE, a broad measure of consumer prices), an updated reading on economic growth, and weekly jobless claims moved up a day. A hot inflation number could undo some of this week's improvement; a soft one could extend it. After that: the Dec 4 jobs report, the Dec 9 Fed decision and November consumer prices on Dec 10.

drivers.title: Stock selloff sent money into bonds
drivers.text: The S&P 500 fell six straight days on worries about AI spending, including about a 2% drop Thursday. Investors moving from stocks into Treasury bonds pushed the 10-year yield from 5.15% to below 5% by Friday, and lenders cut rates 0.12% Friday as they caught up.

drivers.title: Fed officials talking up more hikes
drivers.text: Governor Waller floated a half-point hike in December, St. Louis Fed President Musalem said several more increases are likely by spring, and the October minutes showed almost all officials expect more. A December hike is close to fully expected, which kept rates from falling further early in the week.

drivers.title: Inflation still running hot
drivers.text: October consumer prices beat forecasts for the third month in a row and wholesale prices are up 6.5% from a year ago. Bond investors demand higher yields when inflation eats into what their interest is worth, which limits how far mortgage rates can fall.

drivers.title: Cheaper oil and a cooling economy
drivers.text: U.S. crude fell to its lowest close since late August, factory surveys in New York and Philadelphia weakened, builder confidence hit its lowest since 2012, and consumers lowered their inflation expectations to 3.7%. Softer growth and cooler inflation worries help pull yields and mortgage rates down.

drivers.title: Wide gap between mortgage rates and Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat about 2.19% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 17, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%. That cushion let lenders hold rates steady during last week's selloff and gives them room to lower rates as bonds rally.

talkingPoints.buyers: Rates dropped this week, with the daily 30-year average falling to 7.33% from 7.50%, mostly because investors moved money from stocks into bonds. That improvement can reverse quickly if stocks bounce or Wednesday's inflation report runs hot, and a December Fed hike is still widely expected. If you're shopping or under contract, talk with Stuart about how this week's move affects your payment and your options.
talkingPoints.sellers: Lower rates help buyers' budgets stretch a little further, but rates are still above 7% and builder confidence just hit its lowest since 2012, a sign affordability is still tight. Pricing realistically and being open to helping with a buyer's costs matters more than waiting for rates. Talk with Stuart about what today's rates mean for buyers in your price range.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates fell this week as investors fled stocks for bonds, but a December Fed hike and next Wednesday's inflation report could test that improvement.
